headings.title: Defining Short Bones
headings.content: Bones are classified into several groups based primarily on their overall shape and dimensions. Among these, **short bones** stand out because they are roughly cube-shaped. Their length and width are nearly equal, meaning they do not have a long shaft like the bones in the arms or legs. You can easily picture them as small, sturdy blocks designed to pack tightly together in confined spaces where strength and limited movement are required.

headings.title: Anatomical Locations in the Body
headings.content:
Short bones are not scattered randomly throughout the skeletal system. Instead, clinical anatomy places them exclusively in two specific regions where stability and delicate gliding movements are paramount: the wrist and the ankle.

- **Carpal bones**: The eight small bones making up the wrist, arranged in two rows.
- **Tarsal bones**: The seven small bones forming the posterior half of the foot, including the calcaneus and talus.

headings.title: Internal Histology: Spongy Core and Compact Shell
headings.content: Looking at the outside of a short bone, you will find a thin layer of **compact bone** acting as a protective shell. Beneath this hard exterior lies a core made entirely of **spongy bone**, also known as cancellous or trabecular bone. This spongy interior contains tiny open spaces filled with red bone marrow, which is actively involved in making blood cells. Unlike long bones, short bones do not possess a hollow medullary cavity running down their center.

headings.title: Functional Roles in Movement and Stability
headings.content: Because short bones are tightly packed together by strong ligaments, their primary job is not to act as levers for big movements. Instead, they provide high stability, bear weight, and allow a limited amount of gliding motion between one another. When you write with a pen or walk on uneven ground, your carpals and tarsals shift slightly against each other, absorbing shock and distributing mechanical stress evenly across the joint.

headings.title: Clinical Significance and Common Injuries
headings.content: Injuries to short bones often result from falls onto an outstretched hand or high-impact trauma to the feet. A well-known example is a fracture of the scaphoid bone in the wrist. Midwives and nurses must remember that due to unique blood supply patterns in some short bones, certain fractures carry a high risk of delayed healing or avascular necrosis, where bone tissue dies from a lack of blood flow.
